I thank Ansel, take the bread and the willow-bark, and bless the hospice door before I go. "Keep the book open for Reedholm's names, Brother. I'll write if I can."

Then I set out south on the river road toward the Eel Fork, keeping a steady pace and an eye on the reeds. DM: the carters said Sedge, the boy with the fever, went home sick, so is he the first person I should ask for when I reach Reedholm?

time: 9 hours 30 minutes later: Day 11, 5:11:06 PM
sheet: gained 1 × Willow-bark (twist, for fever)

Yes, Sedge is a good first name to ask for. He is the one the carters can place, a boy who took the sickness home with him. The village will know him, and where he lies will tell you how far the fever has gone. Ask for him and for whoever has been sitting up with the sick. In a place with no healer, that is usually one stubborn woman.

You take Ansel's bread and the dried willow-bark, bless the green door with two fingers and a murmured line of Edda's hymn, and walk out through the south gate. The river road runs along the bank, broad and slow, and the valley flattens as you go. The hills sink to low swells, then to meadow, then to reed-beds and standing water with rooks wheeling over them. You eat as you walk.

Survival (15): you read the road without trouble. At about five in the afternoon you reach a weathered wooden milestone at a fork, carved with a crude eel. This is the Eel Fork. The west branch runs on along the river. The east branch drops onto a raised causeway of packed earth and old timber, running out across the fen with black water on both sides and mist already lifting in the late light.

It's eleven minutes past five on Day 11, with about an hour and a half of daylight left. Reedholm is another day and a half along the causeway. There's a flat dry knoll by the milestone, good enough to camp, with old fire-scars on it. You have all your slots and Channel Divinity, thirty-seven flasks of oil, two lanterns, and rope.

What does Brannoc do?

sheet.name: Brannoc Ashdown
sheet.opening: Brannoc Ashdown, a young human cleric of the Life domain, has been on the road only a few weeks, walking out from Millbrook Landing, the little river town of fishermen and reed-cutters where he grew up. He was orphaned at six when the Grey Fever emptied the houses along the water, and was raised by the temple's old healer, Mother Edda Thorne, who died last winter of old age and left him her plain wooden amulet. He keeps a promise to carry her work to places that have no healer at all. His past (true and not to be contradicted): as a child he sat beside dying neighbors because Edda had too few hands; the night she told him to leave a dying fisherman and rest, he refused, and the man's daughter later thanked him, which is the root of his stubbornness. He hums hymns while he works, is warm and patient, and swore never to let anyone suffer alone again. He is inflexible in his thinking. Open play on a muddy back road at dusk, at the edge of a small, struggling settlement with no priest or healer, its few lanterns lit early and its doors shut. Something has just happened that needs him: a frightened child or farmer hurries out to flag him down, begging for help for sick or wounded people sheltering in a barn, where the trouble is more than illness alone (for example, injuries from a recent attack by raiders or wild beasts, with the threat possibly still near). Brannoc has his mace, chain mail, shield, light crossbow, priest's pack, and 15 gp. Give him a clear, immediate call to act, and room to choose between healing, protecting, and investigating.

features: Divine Domain: Choose one domain related to your deity, such as Life. Each domain is detailed at the end of the class description, and each one provides examples of gods associated with it. Your choice grants you domain spells and other features when you choose it at 1st level. It also grants you additional ways to use Channel Divinity when you gain that feature at 2nd level, and additional benefits at 6th, 8th, and 17th levels.

Domain Spells: Each domain has a list of spells--its domain spells--that you gain at the cleric levels noted in the domain description. Once you gain a domain spell, you always have it prepared, and it doesn't count against the number of spells you can prepare each day. If you have a domain spell that doesn't appear on the cleric spell list, the spell is nonetheless a cleric spell for you.
Bonus Proficiency: When you choose this domain at 1st level, you gain proficiency with heavy armor.

Disciple of Life: Also starting at 1st level, your healing spells are more effective. Whenever you use a spell of 1st level or higher to restore hit points to a creature, the creature regains additional hit points equal to 2 + the spell's level.

Channel Divinity (1/rest): At 2nd level, you gain the ability to channel divine energy directly from your deity, using that energy to fuel magical effects. You start with two such effects: Turn Undead and an effect determined by your domain. Some domains grant you additional effects as you advance in levels, as noted in the domain description. When you use your Channel Divinity, you choose which effect to create. You must then finish a short or long rest to use your Channel Divinity again. Some Channel Divinity effects require saving throws. When you use such an effect from this class, the DC equals your cleric spell save DC. Beginning at 6th level, you can use your Channel Divinity twice between rests, and beginning at 18th level, you can use it three times between rests. When you finish a short or long rest, you regain your expended uses.

Channel Divinity: Turn Undead: As an action, you present your holy symbol and speak a prayer censuring the undead. Each undead that can see or hear you within 30 feet of you must make a Wisdom saving throw. If the creature fails its saving throw, it is turned for 1 minute or until it takes any damage. A turned creature must spend its turns trying to move as far away from you as it can, and it can't willingly move to a space within 30 feet of you. It also can't take reactions. For its action, it can use only the Dash action or try to escape from an effect that prevents it from moving. If there's nowhere to move, the creature can use the Dodge action.

Channel Divinity: Preserve Life: Starting at 2nd level, you can use your Channel Divinity to heal the badly injured. As an action, you present your holy symbol and evoke healing energy that can restore a number of hit points equal to five times your cleric level. Choose any creatures within 30 feet of you, and divide those hit points among them. This feature can restore a creature to no more than half of its hit point maximum. You can't use this feature on an undead or a construct. At level 3: 15 hit points to divide.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

entries.text: notebook: updated Reedholm

Ansel puts the bread and the twist of willow-bark in your hands. You bless the green door and trace the old sign on the lintel. He promises to keep a page of the book open for Reedholm's names. Then you go out by the south gate, past the tired guardsman, who nods you through.

The river road runs low and wide, with the water slow and brown beside it. The land flattens mile by mile. Alders give way to willows, and willows to reed-beds taller than a man. The air turns damp and smells of mud and green rot. You walk at a steady pace, with the second lantern clinking at your pack.

Perception (18): around midday you notice that the reed-beds east of the road have been trampled flat in a long swath, a stone's throw off and running alongside the road. Something heavy and patient has walked there, and more than once. The prints at the edge are blurred by water, bare and long-toed, and old. Nothing moves in them now. You mark the place and go on.

At about four in the afternoon you reach a weathered wooden milestone at a fork, with an eel carved into the post and the words EEL FORK cut below it. The west branch runs on along the river. The east branch drops onto a raised causeway of packed earth and stone between the reeds, and a cold wind off the fen comes up to meet you.

As for Sedge: his is a good name to know, but he is a boy, and he fell ill after he got home. He may be in no state to talk. You would do better to ask for the reeve, or whoever speaks for the village, and find Sedge among the sick.

It's four in the afternoon on Day 11, with about four hours of light left. You have four 1st-level slots, two 2nd-level slots, Channel Divinity and the willow-bark. Reedholm is a day and a half on, and the Black Ford ferry-rope lies somewhere along the causeway. You can camp at the fork or push on along the causeway before dark.

input.description: Fork in the river road south of Stonebridge, marked by a grey wooden milestone carved with an eel. East branch is the causeway to Reedholm (two days from Stonebridge, ferry-rope at the Black Ford); the west branch runs on south. Brannoc reached it about 4 PM on Day 11 and found a lean-to shelter beside it.

entries.text: notebook: created an entry for The Eel Fork; added 2 relationships to The Eel Fork

Ansel takes your hand at the green door and says the book will keep a page open for Reedholm. You bless the lintel with two fingers, and he laughs at you, gently, for blessing a door already blessed.

On your question: Sedge is a good name to carry, but not the first to ask for. He's a boy, and he went home sick, so he may be in no state to answer anything. Ask for whoever speaks for the village, then for Sedge's family. He's the first case you know of, and his family may know how the fever began.

The river road is flat and open. Fields give way to rough pasture, then to alder and willow, and the air turns damp and green. You pass a drover and his geese, and a tinker who warns you, cheerfully, that the fen eats boots. The sun is thin but steady, and nothing troubles you. A little after four, you come to the Eel Fork. A grey wooden milestone leans there with an eel carved down its length, worn nearly smooth. The east branch is a raised causeway of packed earth and stone, running straight out between reed-beds into a flat, pale distance. The west road climbs away into low hills. Beside the milestone someone has built a lean-to of driftwood and thatch, with a ring of black stones for a fire.

The reeds hiss in the wind. Far off over the fen, a thin mist is already rising, though the sun hasn't set.

It's four in the afternoon on Day 11. You have all your slots and Channel Divinity, since you've spent nothing today, plus thirty-seven flasks, two lanterns and 4 gp. The causeway is a day and a half of walking, and you could shelter here tonight or push on along it while the light holds.

A village in a fever will also take a stranger more kindly if he comes asking for a sick boy by name. The carters said his mother keeps the first house on the causeway, so you won't have to hunt for it.

You bless the green door and Ansel grips your hand. Then you walk. The river road runs south through a widening, flatter country of willows and wet pasture. The air gets damp and smells of mud and cut reeds. You eat Ansel's bread by the roadside and chew a sliver of willow-bark for the taste of it.

Survival (13): the road is plain and the milestone is easy to spot, so you reach it with the afternoon still bright. It is a squat wooden post, weathered grey and carved with an eel on one face and a reed on the other. The road splits here. The west fork goes on south along the river to country you don't know, and the east fork drops onto a raised causeway of packed earth and brush that runs out across the fen. Beyond it the land goes flat and silver for miles, with reed-beds, black water, and low mist. The wind is quiet. You can hear frogs, and nothing else.

It's a quarter past four on Day 11. Reedholm is a day and a half of causeway from here, with a ferry-rope at the Black Ford. You've got your prayers full, thirty-seven flasks, and four hours of light. You could go on and camp on the causeway, or turn back to Stonebridge's last milestone-hut a mile north and start fresh at dawn.

What does Brannoc do?

sheet.name: Brannoc Ashdown
sheet.opening: Brannoc Ashdown, a young human cleric of the Life domain, has been on the road only a few weeks, walking out from Millbrook Landing, the little river town of fishermen and reed-cutters where he grew up. He was orphaned at six when the Grey Fever emptied the houses along the water, and was raised by the temple's old healer, Mother Edda Thorne, who died last winter of old age and left him her plain wooden amulet. He keeps a promise to carry her work to places that have no healer at all. His past (true and not to be contradicted): as a child he sat beside dying neighbors because Edda had too few hands; the night she told him to leave a dying fisherman and rest, he refused, and the man's daughter later thanked him, which is the root of his stubbornness. He hums hymns while he works, is warm and patient, and swore never to let anyone suffer alone again. He is inflexible in his thinking. Open play on a muddy back road at dusk, at the edge of a small, struggling settlement with no priest or healer, its few lanterns lit early and its doors shut. Something has just happened that needs him: a frightened child or farmer hurries out to flag him down, begging for help for sick or wounded people sheltering in a barn, where the trouble is more than illness alone (for example, injuries from a recent attack by raiders or wild beasts, with the threat possibly still near). Brannoc has his mace, chain mail, shield, light crossbow, priest's pack, and 15 gp. Give him a clear, immediate call to act, and room to choose between healing, protecting, and investigating.

features: Divine Domain: Choose one domain related to your deity, such as Life. Each domain is detailed at the end of the class description, and each one provides examples of gods associated with it. Your choice grants you domain spells and other features when you choose it at 1st level. It also grants you additional ways to use Channel Divinity when you gain that feature at 2nd level, and additional benefits at 6th, 8th, and 17th levels.

Domain Spells: Each domain has a list of spells--its domain spells--that you gain at the cleric levels noted in the domain description. Once you gain a domain spell, you always have it prepared, and it doesn't count against the number of spells you can prepare each day. If you have a domain spell that doesn't appear on the cleric spell list, the spell is nonetheless a cleric spell for you.
Bonus Proficiency: When you choose this domain at 1st level, you gain proficiency with heavy armor.

Disciple of Life: Also starting at 1st level, your healing spells are more effective. Whenever you use a spell of 1st level or higher to restore hit points to a creature, the creature regains additional hit points equal to 2 + the spell's level.

Channel Divinity (1/rest): At 2nd level, you gain the ability to channel divine energy directly from your deity, using that energy to fuel magical effects. You start with two such effects: Turn Undead and an effect determined by your domain. Some domains grant you additional effects as you advance in levels, as noted in the domain description. When you use your Channel Divinity, you choose which effect to create. You must then finish a short or long rest to use your Channel Divinity again. Some Channel Divinity effects require saving throws. When you use such an effect from this class, the DC equals your cleric spell save DC. Beginning at 6th level, you can use your Channel Divinity twice between rests, and beginning at 18th level, you can use it three times between rests. When you finish a short or long rest, you regain your expended uses.

Channel Divinity: Turn Undead: As an action, you present your holy symbol and speak a prayer censuring the undead. Each undead that can see or hear you within 30 feet of you must make a Wisdom saving throw. If the creature fails its saving throw, it is turned for 1 minute or until it takes any damage. A turned creature must spend its turns trying to move as far away from you as it can, and it can't willingly move to a space within 30 feet of you. It also can't take reactions. For its action, it can use only the Dash action or try to escape from an effect that prevents it from moving. If there's nowhere to move, the creature can use the Dodge action.

Channel Divinity: Preserve Life: Starting at 2nd level, you can use your Channel Divinity to heal the badly injured. As an action, you present your holy symbol and evoke healing energy that can restore a number of hit points equal to five times your cleric level. Choose any creatures within 30 feet of you, and divide those hit points among them. This feature can restore a creature to no more than half of its hit point maximum. You can't use this feature on an undead or a construct. At level 3: 15 hit points to divide.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

spellcasting.notes: Prepare up to 6 spells from the whole cleric list after a long rest (domain spells are always prepared and don't count).
